front: Distinguish periodic motion from oscillatory motion.
back: Periodic motion repeats itself at regular intervals of time (insect on a ramp, child on a step, bouncing ball). Oscillatory (vibratory) motion is to-and-fro motion about an equilibrium position inside the path — no net force there, and a restoring force returns the body to it (cradle, swing, pendulum). EVERY oscillatory motion is periodic, but not every periodic motion is oscillatory (uniform circular motion is periodic, not oscillatory).

front: Give everyday and physical examples of oscillatory systems.
back: Vibrating strings of a sitar/guitar/violin, drum membranes, telephone and loudspeaker diaphragms, the vibration of air molecules carrying sound, atoms vibrating in solids (average energy proportional to temperature), and AC voltage oscillating about zero. Any material medium is a collection of coupled oscillators; their collective oscillation gives rise to waves.

front: Define period, frequency and their relation and units.
back: Period T: the smallest interval of time after which motion repeats; SI unit is the second (a quartz-crystal period is in µs; Mercury's orbital period is 88 days; Halley's comet 76 years). Frequency ν = 1/T; SI unit s⁻¹ = hertz (Hz), 1 Hz = 1 oscillation per second. Frequency need not be an integer.

front: What is meant by 'displacement' in this chapter?
back: Displacement means the change with time of ANY physical property under consideration — not just position. Examples: position of a spring block, angle of a pendulum from the vertical, voltage across a capacitor, pressure in a sound wave, electric/magnetic fields in a light wave. It can be positive or negative and is a periodic function of time.

front: Write the simplest periodic functions and their period.
back: f(t) = A cos ωt (Eq 13.3a) with period T = 2π/ω (Eq 13.3b), so f(t) = f(t + T). The sine function and any linear combination f(t) = A sin ωt + B cos ωt (Eq 13.3c) are periodic with the same period T.

front: How is f(t) = A sin ωt + B cos ωt rewritten as a single sinusoid?
back: Set A = D cos φ and B = D sin φ; then f(t) = D sin(ωt + φ) (Eq 13.3d) with amplitude D = √(A² + B²) and phase constant tan φ = B/A. The combination is periodic with the same period T = 2π/ω.

front: State Fourier's theorem relevant to periodic motion.
back: Any periodic function can be expressed as a superposition of sine and cosine functions of different time periods with suitable coefficients (Fourier, 1768–1830). This is why sinusoidal components are the natural building blocks for analysing periodic phenomena.

front: Which of these are periodic: sinωt+cosωt, sinωt+cos2ωt+sin4ωt, e^(−ωt), log(ωt)?
back: sinωt + cosωt = √2 sin(ωt + π/4): periodic, T = 2π/ω. sinωt + cos2ωt + sin4ωt: periods T₀, T₀/2, T₀/4 (T₀ = 2π/ω); repeats at their least common period 2π/ω — periodic. e^(−ωt): decreases monotonically, never repeats — NON-periodic. log(ωt): grows monotonically and diverges — NON-periodic, cannot represent a physical displacement. (Example 13.2.)

front: Define simple harmonic motion (SHM).
back: SHM is a motion in which the displacement is a sinusoidal function of time: x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ) with constants A, ω, φ (Eq 13.4). It is NOT just any periodic motion — it is the simplest oscillatory motion, equivalent to a restoring force proportional to displacement. Uniform circular motion is periodic but not oscillatory.

front: Define amplitude, phase, phase constant and angular frequency.
back: Amplitude A: magnitude of maximum displacement, displacement varies between +A and −A. Phase (ωt + φ): fixes position and velocity at time t. Phase constant φ: value of phase at t = 0, determined from initial displacement if amplitude is known. Angular frequency ω = 2π/T = 2πν (Eq 13.7), SI unit rad s⁻¹. Same A and φ with larger ω gives a shorter period/higher frequency.

front: Show that SHM is the projection of uniform circular motion.
back: A particle P moving uniformly (angular speed ω) on a reference circle of radius A with initial angle φ has position vector making angle ωt + φ after time t. Its x-projection, x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ), is exactly SHM (observed when a rotating ball viewed edge-on appears to oscillate along a diameter). The y-projection gives y = A sin(ωt + φ), the same motion with phase shifted by π/2.

front: Write the SHM equations for a particle whose reference motion (a) starts at 45°, opposite/anticlockwise, T = 4 s, and (b) starts at 90°, clockwise, T = 30 s.
back: (a) x(t) = A cos(2πt/4 + π/4) = A cos(πt/2 + π/4) — SHM, amplitude A, period 4 s, initial phase π/4. (b) x(t) = B cos(π/2 − 2πt/30) = B sin(πt/15) = B cos(πt/15 − π/2) — SHM, amplitude B, period 30 s, initial phase −π/2. (Example 13.4.)

front: Write the velocity and acceleration of an SHM and their phase relations.
back: From uniform circular motion, v = ωA; the projection velocity is v(t) = −ωA sin(ωt + φ) = dx/dt (Eq 13.9, 13.10). Projecting the centripetal acceleration a = ω²A toward the centre: a(t) = −ω²A cos(ωt + φ) = −ω²x(t) (Eq 13.11), also dv/dt (Eq 13.12). So acceleration ∝ displacement and directed to the mean position; speed max at x = 0, zero at extremes. With φ = 0, v leads x by π/2 and a leads x by π (Fig 13.13).

front: State the force law for SHM and the corresponding period.
back: F(t) = −mω²x(t) = −kx(t) (Eq 13.13) with k = mω² (Eq 13.14a) and ω = √(k/m) (Eq 13.14b). The restoring force is always directed towards the mean position. SHM can be defined equivalently by the displacement law (13.4) or the force law (13.13). A linear harmonic oscillator has F ∝ x; real anharmonic oscillators have extra terms in x², x³ making them non-linear.

front: How are kinetic, potential and total energy distributed in SHM?
back: K = ½mv² = ½kA² sin²(ωt + φ) (Eq 13.15): zero at extremes, maximum at mean position, period T/2. U = ½kx² = ½kA² cos²(ωt + φ) (Eq 13.16–13.17): zero at mean, maximum at extremes, period T/2. Total E = U + K = ½kA² (Eq 13.18) is constant (conservative spring force). At x = 0 all energy is kinetic; at x = ±A all is potential.

front: Derive the simple-pendulum period for small oscillations.
back: Forces on the bob: tension T along the string and weight mg. Resolving mg gives mg cos θ radially (with T providing the centripetal force) and mg sin θ tangentially. The restoring torque about the support is τ = −L(mg sin θ) (Eq 13.19); Newton's rotational law τ = Iα gives α = −(mgL/I) sin θ (Eq 13.22). For small θ, sin θ ≈ θ, so α = −(mgL/I)θ — identical in form to SHM. Then ω = √(mgL/I), T = 2π√(I/mgL) (Eq 13.25); for a massless string I = mL² and T = 2π√(L/g) (Eq 13.26).

front: Give Table 13.1 (θ in degrees, radians and sinθ) and its significance.
back: θ(deg): 0, 5, 10, 15, 20; θ(rad): 0, 0.087, 0.174, 0.262, 0.349; sinθ: 0, 0.087, 0.174, 0.259, 0.342. Up to about 20°, sinθ ≈ θ (angle in radians) to good accuracy — this is the small-angle approximation that makes the pendulum SHM (Eq 13.23–13.24).

front: Solver's note: which of four given x–t plots are periodic, and with what period?
back: Plots (b) and (d) are periodic, each with period T = 2 s; plots (a) and (c) are non-periodic. (Exercise 13.3.) A periodic plot repeats its shape exactly after a fixed time interval — here only (b) and (d) do.

front: Which a–x relations represent SHM: a = 0.7x, a = −200x², a = −10x, a = 100x³?
back: Only a = −10x: the SHM signature is a = −ω²x — acceleration proportional in magnitude to displacement and oppositely directed. The relations a = 0.7x (wrong sign) and the quadratic/cubic relations (wrong dependence on x) are not SHM. (Exercise 13.6.)

front: Compare the period of a single spring–mass (case a) with two identical masses on the same spring (case b).
back: Case (a): one end clamped, force F at the free end gives extension x = F/k, period T = 2π√(m/k). Case (b): both ends of the same spring free, each end holding a mass m with force F — the centre stays at rest and each half behaves like a spring of constant 2k, so each mass oscillates with T = 2π√(m/2k). (Exercise 13.13.)

front: What is the period of a pendulum of length l hanging in a car moving with speed v on a circular track of radius R?
back: The bob experiences vertical g and a horizontal centrifugal/pseudo acceleration v²/R. The effective gravitational field is √(g² + (v²/R)²), so the pendulum oscillates as if g were replaced by this: T = 2π√(l/√(g² + v⁴/R²)). (Exercise 13.16.)

front: Give the SHM period for a floating cylinder and for a U-tube mercury column.
back: Floating cork cylinder (base A, height h, density ρ) in liquid of density ρ₁: the extra buoyant force −ρ₁gAx is the restoring force; a = −(ρ₁g/ρh)x, so ω² = ρ₁g/(ρh) and T = 2π√(ρh/ρ₁g) (Exercise 13.17). U-tube mercury column of total length L = 2h (height h each arm): excess weight 2xρgA drives it to equilibrium; a = −(g/h)x, so T = 2π√(h/g) = 2π√(L/2g) (Exercise 13.18).
